title: Assessing metacognition-based student feedback literacy for academic writing

in student feedback literacy, respectively. Research has also shown that students with enhanced knowledge of features of good writing 
(i.e., a type of metacognitive task knowledge in student feedback literacy) are able to generate internal feedback to improve their 
writing. For instance, the two low-proficiency EFL students in Ma and Teng’s (2020) study learned from exemplars various features of 
good academic writing and applied them to their own writing to improve its quality. It has also been found that EFL writers who 
consciously compare their own writing against external references such as the writing of peers or assessment criteria are able to better 
revise their writing (Ma, 2021). If learners are able to activate the strategy of using comparison to generate quality internal feedback (i. 
e., a kind of metacognitive skill/strategy in student feedback literacy), then they are more likely to improve their learning performance 
(Nicol, 2020). Finally, metacognitive knowledge and skills (or lack thereof) influence students’ engagement with writing feedback. 
Zhang and Hyland (2018) investigated the ways EFL students engage with different sources of feedback, as well as the impact of such 
engagement on writing over time. They found that factors such as utilization of a repertoire of learning strategies (e.g., metacognitive 
strategies) and motivational beliefs influenced student engagement with external feedback and their writing quality. These two factors 
can be regarded as metacognitive strategies and person knowledge, respectively, in student feedback literacy. The metacognitive 
strategies, related strategy knowledge, and person knowledge are important to learners’ interpretation and use of feedback for writing

specifically, to feedback-related writing processes, leading to potential writing outcomes. Therefore, our focus was directed towards a 
quantitative analysis that investigates the relationship between MSFL and writing outcomes, rather than a qualitative analysis of the 
learners’ writing processes. This approach allows for a more comprehensive understanding of student feedback literacy from a met- 
acognitive perspective and its impact on students’ writing performance. 
We aim to answer the following two research questions: 
 
1. Is the MSFL a psychometrically reliable and valid instrument to measure metacognition in student feedback literacy? If yes, what 
structural model can represent the dimensions of MSFL? 
2. Does MSFL predict academic writing? If yes, to what extent? 
 
3. Method 
 
3.1. Participants 
 
The participants were 708 second-year students from a university in China, of whom 365 were men and 343 were women. Their 
ages ranged from 19 to 21 (Mage = 19.91, SD = 1.05). They were from different majors, including transportation, engineering, 
computer science, marketing, and management. They were from 16 classes, and their first language was Mandarin Chinese. Second- 
year students were chosen because they were enrolled in the Academic Writing in English (AWE) course. The learners had at least 10 
years of English learning experience. In their first year of study, they attended an English writing course named Basic English Writing 
(BEW). There were some differences between AWE and BEW. For example, AWE focuses on proving a theory or viewpoint in one way 
or another and emphasizes one specific subject, like science. BEW focuses on general subjects of writing. They had limited experience

enable student writers to participate in feedback processes to monitor and regulate their writing processes. 
Three experts with good knowledge of metacognition and student feedback literacy checked the content of the survey and agreed 
that most of the items reflected the different components of metacognition in student feedback literacy. As mentioned, they pointed out 
that the knowledge of learning through assessment should be placed under the knowing dimension, given that the being dimension 
mainly encapsulates motivational self-knowledge. Four teachers who had experience in EFL writing agreed on the items for under- 
standing feedback and writing. We also piloted the survey with 10 EFL students. They expressed that the items were clear. We deleted 
six items based on comments from the writing researchers, teachers, and students. The final survey had 53 items (see Appendix). The 
Cronbach’s alpha for the different components of the survey ranged from.82 to.86, indicating sound reliability. 
 
3.3. Academic writing (AW) test 
 
This is a semester-end standardized test for assessing the academic writing performance of all the students enrolled in the AWE 
course. This test evaluated student writers’ ability to understand topic sentences, provide details, outline problems, and provide ar- 
guments based on their own knowledge or experience. This test included five parts, with 20 points allocated to each part, for a 
maximum of 100 points. The first part assessed learners’ ability to recognize topic sentences. The learners read the sentences and 
decided which one was the topic sentence. There were 10 groups of sentences in this part. The second part assessed learners’ ability to

We then validated the first-order model of validating the three dimensions, i.e., knowing, being, and doing (Fig. 4). The results also 
showed an acceptable model fit (χ2/df = 2.873; p < .001; RMSEA =.080, SRMR=.028; CFI =.971; TLI =.959). The results provided 
evidence for the validity of the internal structure of the first-order model of validating the three dimensions of MSFL to the 10 factors. 
We then validated the one-factor second-order model (Fig. 5). Fig. 5 shows the standardized results. Again, the standardized es- 
timate loadings were all higher than.50, indicating an acceptable effect size (Raykov & Marcoulides, 2008). The results also showed an 
acceptable model fit (χ2/df = 2.813; p < .001; RMSEA =.059, SRMR=.056; CFI =.927; TLI =.919). The results provided evidence for 
the validity of the internal structure of the second-order model. This model showed better model fit than the previous two models. This 
is evidence for the validity of metacognition in student feedback literacy as a hierarchical construct explaining the 10 factors as an 
appropriate model fit in the present study. 
 
4.3. The predictive effects of MSFL on AW 
 
To answer the second question of whether MSFL predicts academic writing (AW), we evaluated the overall results of MSFL on 
academic writing performance. The results are shown in Fig. 6. The results showed an acceptable model fit (χ2/df = 2.953; p < .001;

Another important variable that influences performance in academic writing is motivation. Self-perceived motivation belongs to 
the person knowledge of student writers (Victori, 1999). The findings supported previous research by highlighting the essential role of 
person knowledge, especially self-perceived motivation, in fostering active engagement in writing and enhancing students’ writing 
outcomes (Ma & Teng, 2020). Metacognitive knowledge is not only cognitively oriented, but also motivational, with the motivational 
aspect energizing the processes of self-regulation (Wenden, 1998). Motivation shapes student engagement in self-regulatory processes 
(Bakhtiar & Hadwin, 2022). It is likely that the learners’ self-regulation of academic writing was enhanced by self-perceived moti- 
vation through fueling their seeking, generating, processing, and using of feedback. Such enhanced self-regulation may contribute to 
writing performance. Adding to Yu et al.’s (2022) finding that managing affect is an important component of L2 student writers’ 
literary feedback, our study showed that self-perceived motivation might enable student writers to participate actively in a series of

feedback-related activities to energize the self-regulation process and thus enhance writing outcomes. 
The predictive effects of feedback-related monitoring strategies (FRMS) reflect the importance of self-monitoring in writing (Teng 
et al., 2022). As argued by Qin and Zhang (2019), EFL learners’ metacognitive writing strategies, such as planning, monitoring, and 
evaluating, were significantly associated with their writing performance (see also Teng & Huang, 2019; Teng, 2020). The role of 
metacognitive regulation strategies in writing was also highlighted in Teng (2016, 2020). However, those studies did not specifically 
focus on feedback-related planning, monitoring, and evaluating strategies in writing. In particular, the present study shows that 
monitoring strategies involving the generation of internal feedback are especially important to writing performance. This finding can 
be supported by the argument that the generation of internal feedback is key to improving learning performance (Nicol, 2020; Yan & 
Carless, 2021), including writing (Andrade & Brooke, 2010). Based on the predictive effects of feedback-related monitoring strategies

of feedback on academic writing. Focusing on either one or two elements of the four core activities involved in feedback processes, 
qualitative research on student feedback literacy has shown that learners who adopt various strategies to seek, generate, process, or use 
feedback tend to generate better writing outcomes (Ma, 2021; Ma & Teng, 2020; Ma et al., 2021; Zhang & Hyland, 2018), indicating 
the importance of the underlying strategy knowledge to writing performance. Our study supported this finding based on quantitative 
data but underscored the impact on writing performance of knowledge related to strategy use in the entire feedback processes (i.e., all 
four core activities in the feedback processes). 
 
5.3. Limitations and implications 
 
There are some limitations that we would like to acknowledge. First, even though the findings showed the empirical validity of 
MSFL, the various components that we attempted to cover may not be sufficient to reflect the complex nature of metacognition-based 
student feedback literacy in academic writing. Second, the findings were mainly based on self-report data. The scale may not fully 
reflect learners’ feedback literacy in academic writing. Third, the academic writing test did not cover all genres of writing. The 
predictive effects of different components may be different in different genres of writing. In addition, while the writing test does focus 
on certain aspects of academic writing such as reading comprehension, sentence and paragraph structure, and genre knowledge, it may

experience and language proficiency level, were not controlled in exploring the dynamic relationship with student feedback literacy.
